timeline.title: Born in London
timeline.text: Augusta Ada Byron was born on 10 December 1815. She was the only child of the poet Lord Byron and his wife Anne Isabella Milbanke, known as Lady Byron.

timeline.title: Her parents part
timeline.text: In January 1816 Lady Byron left with five-week-old Ada for her parents' home. In April Lord Byron signed a deed of separation and soon left England for good. Ada never had a relationship with her father.

timeline.title: Her father dies abroad
timeline.text: Lord Byron died in Greece in April 1824, when Ada was eight. Her mother had her taught mathematics and science from an early age, which was unusual for a girl at the time.

timeline.title: Flyology
timeline.text: At twelve, Ada started a project she called Flyology. She studied how birds fly and planned to build wings, working through the problem like an engineer.

timeline.title: A long illness
timeline.text: In June 1829 she was left unable to walk after an illness with measles. She spent nearly a year resting in bed. By 1831 she could walk again with crutches.

timeline.title: A gift for mathematics
timeline.text: Around 1832 her talent for mathematics began to show. She was taught privately by tutors including William Frend, the doctor William King and the scientist Mary Somerville. She never went to school or university.

timeline.title: Meeting Babbage
timeline.text: On 5 June 1833, at one of his Saturday evening parties, Ada met the mathematician and inventor Charles Babbage. Mary Somerville, their mutual friend, made the introduction. The two became lifelong friends.

timeline.title: The Difference Engine
timeline.text: Later that June, Babbage invited her to see a working part of his Difference Engine, a machine for calculating tables of numbers. She was fascinated by it and called it the "gem of all mechanism".

timeline.title: Marriage
timeline.text: On 8 July 1835 Ada married William King. He was not related to her earlier tutor of the same name.

timeline.title: A family
timeline.text: Ada and William had three children: Byron in 1836, Anne Isabella (Annabella) in 1837 and Ralph in 1839.

timeline.title: Babbage's new engine
timeline.text: Babbage first described the Analytical Engine in 1837. Unlike his earlier machine, it was designed to follow instructions on punched cards, with a store for numbers and a mill to calculate. From 1837 to 1840 he wrote about two dozen sample programs for it in his own notebooks. They were never published.

timeline.title: Countess of Lovelace
timeline.text: Her husband was made Earl of Lovelace in 1838, and Ada became the Countess of Lovelace. This is the name history remembers her by.

timeline.title: Lessons by letter
timeline.text: In 1840 and 1841 she took an informal course by letter with the mathematics professor Augustus De Morgan. Her letters show her growing into a capable mathematician who was willing to question her teacher. They survive in the Bodleian Library in Oxford.

timeline.title: The Turin lecture
timeline.text: Babbage gave a talk on the Analytical Engine in Turin. It was the only public explanation of the engine he ever gave. A young engineer, Luigi Menabrea, wrote it up in French.

timeline.title: Menabrea's paper
timeline.text: Menabrea's French description of the engine was published in the Bibliotheque Universelle de Geneve in October 1842.

timeline.title: The translation
timeline.text: The scientist Charles Wheatstone asked Ada to translate Menabrea's paper into English. Babbage later wrote that he suggested she add notes of her own, an idea she took up at once. She worked on it for about nine months, writing to Babbage as she went.

timeline.title: Note G
timeline.text: Her seventh note, Note G, set out in full detail how the engine could compute the Bernoulli numbers. It is often called the first published computer program, though the engine was never built, so it was never run. Babbage wrote that he had offered to do the algebra for this part, and that she sent it back after finding a serious mistake in his work. A modern check found a small error in one step of the printed table.

timeline.title: The Notes are published
timeline.text: The translation appeared in Richard Taylor's Scientific Memoirs in the summer of 1843. Sources give the month as August or September. She signed only her initials, A. A. L. Her seven notes, A to G, were about three times as long as the paper itself.

timeline.title: Enchantress of Number
timeline.text: In a letter that year, Babbage called her "The Enchantress of Number". The name has stayed with her.

timeline.title: New questions
timeline.text: She visited the scientist Andrew Crosse to learn about electrical experiments, and wrote a review of a book on magnetism by Karl von Reichenbach. The review was never published.

timeline.title: Debts
timeline.text: In the late 1840s she lost large sums betting on horse races. In 1851 a plan with friends to build a mathematical model for betting failed and left her thousands of pounds in debt.

timeline.title: An early death
timeline.text: After months of illness, Ada died of cancer on 27 November 1852, aged 36. At her own request she was buried next to her father at the Church of St Mary Magdalene in Hucknall, Nottinghamshire.

timeline.title: Babbage remembers
timeline.text: In his memoir, Babbage wrote that the choice of examples in the Notes was entirely hers, and that she had entered fully into almost all the hard questions about the engine.

timeline.title: Lady Lovelace's objection
timeline.text: In his paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence, Alan Turing answered her line that the engine could not originate anything. He called it "Lady Lovelace's objection" and argued that machines could still surprise us.

timeline.title: The Notes return
timeline.text: More than a century after her death, her Notes were reprinted in B. V. Bowden's book Faster Than Thought, and a new generation of computer builders read them.

timeline.title: A language named Ada
timeline.text: The US Department of Defense approved the standard for a new programming language named Ada on her birthday. Its number, MIL-STD-1815, honours the year she was born.

timeline.title: The first programmer debate
timeline.text: Historians still disagree about how much of the programming was hers. Allan Bromley wrote in 1990 that all but one of the programs in the Notes had been prepared by Babbage years earlier. Others, such as Stephen Wolfram, argue she drove the Bernoulli work. Doron Swade says she published the first program rather than wrote it, but credits her with seeing that a machine could go beyond number.

timeline.title: Ada Lovelace Day
timeline.text: Suw Charman-Anderson started Ada Lovelace Day, held on the second Tuesday of October, to celebrate women in science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

timeline.title: Two hundred years
timeline.text: For her 200th birthday, the Bodleian Library, the Science Museum in London and the Computer History Museum held exhibitions of her papers and work. Her mathematical papers began to be put online.

works.title: Sketch of the Analytical Engine (translation)
works.text: Her English translation of Luigi Menabrea's French paper on Babbage's Analytical Engine, published in Scientific Memoirs and signed A. A. L.

works.title: Note A: more than a calculator
works.text: Explains how the Analytical Engine differs from the Difference Engine, compares its punched cards to the Jacquard loom, and suggests it could work on anything whose rules can be written as symbols, even music.

works.title: Notes B, C and D: tables of operations
works.text: Show, with detailed diagrams, how numbers move between the engine's store and mill, and which operation acts at each step. Note D works through solving two equations in full.

works.title: Notes E and F: cycles
works.text: Introduce the idea of a cycle, a group of operations repeated more than once, much like a loop in a modern program, and show how it saves cards and effort.

works.title: Note G: the Bernoulli numbers
works.text: A step-by-step method for the engine to compute the Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published computer program. Babbage had written unpublished programs from 1837, and historians disagree on how much of this one was hers.

works.title: Note G: what a machine cannot do
works.text: Warns against overrating the engine: it can only do what we know how to order it to do. Alan Turing answered this idea in 1950 as "Lady Lovelace's objection".

works.title: Letters with Augustus De Morgan
works.text: Her informal mathematics course by letter in 1840 and 1841, now in the Lovelace Byron papers at the Bodleian Library, with images and transcripts online.

works.title: Flyology
works.text: A childhood project at twelve to study how birds fly and design wings, an early sign of her engineering way of thinking.

works.title: Review of Reichenbach's Researches on Magnetism
works.text: A review she wrote of a book on magnetism by Karl von Reichenbach. It was never published.
